A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. When a life insurance check arrives, suddenly possibility comes with a price. As each family member reaches for a different dream, they must confront what a better life really means – and what America is willing to share. Both tender and electrifying, A Raisin in the Sun celebrates Black joy, resilience and family while facing the brutal realities of segregation and discrimination. A landmark of American theater, it made history as the first Broadway play written by an African American woman (Lorraine Hansberry), the first Broadway play directed by an African American man (Lloyd Richards), and the first commercially produced Broadway drama to center Black life. TDPS Assistant Professor KenYatta Rogers (director of Stick Fly, Men on Boats , Metamorphoses and Home ) directs this enduring American classic. events.description: Explore the remarkable story of bison. These iconic animals shaped North American landscapes for more than 100,000 years and anchored Indigenous lifeways for generations. Pushed to the brink of extinction in the 19th century, bison survived thanks to dedicated conservation efforts. Today, they stand strong as an enduring symbol of survival and resilience. The Bison: Standing Strong exhibit invites you into this incredible journey. Explore a full-sized bull bison specimen, the six-foot-wide skull of an ancient bison ancestor, an immersive soundscape, multimedia, cutting-edge scientific research, and Native objects and stories shared in collaboration with community members. Experience the deep history of America’s national mammal and discover the hopeful future being built for generations to come.

events.title: Bronze Bison: Exhibit
events.address: 10th St. & Constitution Ave., NW, Washington, DC 20560
events.description: More than 100 years ago, real bison grazed outside the Smithsonian Castle building. Bison are returning in a bold new way! Three larger-than-life bronze bison, created by sculptor Gary Staab, find a permanent home outside the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. These towering sculptures of a bull, cow, and calf are at 125 percent scale and modeled after taxidermy specimens seen at the Smithsonian between 1888 and 1957. The original bison diorama introduced generations of visitors to an animal and a prairie landscape they had never seen and helped spark the bison conservation movement. events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Civil War History in Oakton and Vienna
events.description: Greater Oakton Community Association invites history enthusiasts to join a narrated historic bus tour led by acclaimed local historian Jim Lewis on from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Please arrive at 9:00 a.m. at Oakton Community Park at 2841 Hunter Mill Road (next to the old schoolhouse and roundabout) for Jim Lewis's opening comments, then board the bus for departure by 9:30 a.m. The tour will end at 1:00 p.m. This 3.5-hour journey spans Fairfax County's history from its formation in 1742 through the early 1900s, focusing on sites primarily on or just off Hunter Mill Road. Participants hear stories of where the old mills and roads were located and learn about famed military figures (particularly from the Civil War era) and colorful residents who graced the area. Numerous period photographs support the narrative, bringing history to life. Walking requirements are minimal, although one segment involves going down a slight grassy decline. The tour runs rain or shine. Snacks and water are included. Cost is $45 per seat. In the event of cancellation, refunds are provided if a replacement is found for the seat; a wait list is maintained for this purpose. There are 23 seats on the bus. Special "Event Pricing" is offered for the award-winning "Danger Between the Lines" DVD and tour-related illustrated books, available for purchase with cash only. Narrated Historic Bus Tour with Jim Lewis combines local history education, community connection, and immersive storytelling in Fairfax County, Virginia. Questions? Email contact@greateroakton.com . events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. events.title: Entertainment Nation
events.address: 14th Street and Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, DC 20560
events.description: Entertainment has the power to captivate, inspire and transform us. It brings us together. We share it when we spontaneously recite lines from a favorite movie, dance to the same groove or recreate a national sports moment on a neighborhood street. It can also spur critical conversations, expose divides, and foster important historical change. Through the National Museum of American History’s extraordinary collection of theater, music, sports, movie and television objects, the exhibition features a powerful, ever-changing selection of objects and interactive experiences. Through the objects and their stories, the exhibition explores how, for more than 150 years, entertainment has provided a forum for important national conversations about who we are, and who we want to be.

events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn
events.description: Friends Gather Here: A Legacy of Two Communities at Woodlawn explores the powerful history of Quaker families who came to Woodlawn to establish an antislavery community rooted in equality and nonviolence. Through innovative farming and free labor, they sought to demonstrate an alternative to slavery in Virginia, settling alongside a small, established free Black community already living in the area. This exhibit examines the parallel lives, shared aspirations, and evolving relationships between these neighboring communities. As part of the Virginia 250th commemoration, Friends Gather Here invites us to reflect on this quiet revolution and examine our nation’s foundational ideals. events.title: In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness
events.address: 14th Street and Constitution Avenue, N.W., Washington, DC 20560
events.description: The Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History will lead the nation’s 250th anniversary celebrations with a bold, immersive exhibition exploring the ideals of the Declaration of Independence. In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness will span three floors and 300,000 square feet, featuring 250 significant objects, including the desk Jefferson used to draft the Declaration of Independence. Another noteworthy artifact is the only surviving ship of the early U.S. Navy, the gunboat Philadelphia . This National Historic Landmark helped stall British forces and now will undergo an on-site conservation to preserve it for future generations. Visitors and online audiences can engage with both the triumphs and challenges of America’s journey through a year-long series of dynamic programs, from hands-on activities and theatrical performances to educational tools and virtual field trips for classrooms across the country. The museum's Semiquincentennial exhibitions and events begin in the spring of 2026, welcoming all Americans to reflect on the enduring and sometimes delayed or denied promises that surround the ongoing pursuit of life, liberty and happiness.

events.title: Indecent: The True Story of a Little Jewish Play
events.description: ASL Sign Interpreted Performance and Afterword discussion on Friday, November 20 . Written by Paula Vogel, Score and Original Music by Lisa Gutkin and Aaron Halva Directed by Sasha Olinick Performances will be held in the Theatre Arts Arena on the Montgomery College Rockville campus. In 1906 a young, up and coming Jewish/Polish writer, Sholem Asch, penned “God of Vengeance”, a play attacking religious hypocrisy and lovingly depicting a romantic relationship between two women. The play quickly became a hit as it toured throughout Europe and was translated from its original Yiddish into several different languages. But in America, when an English translation opened on Broadway in 1923, the play was quickly shut down and the cast, director and producer were jailed and prosecuted for violating obscenity laws. Indecent, by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Paula Vogel, charts the history of this incendiary drama and the path of the artists who risked their careers and lives to perform it. INDECENT is presented by arrangement with Concord Theatricals on behalf of Dramatists Play Service. Indecent is recommended for mature audiences and teenagers aged 13 and older due to adult themes and historical prejudice.

events.title: Miguel Braceli: UNBURIAL (exhibition)
events.address: St. John's College, 60 College Avenue, Annapolis, MD 21401
events.description: Unburial treats absence as a site for learning and reflection. The void left by the Liberty Tree becomes more than metaphor: an art intervention transforms it into a place to be repurposed and reclaimed through rituals and celebrations that probe what freedom means today. On the front lawn, where the Liberty Tree once stood, the artist Miguel Braceli has installed a 40'-diameter circle of cemetery vases filled with common wildflowers. It calls attention to the tree's absence and reclaims it as a tree for all people, not just the privileged and elite (e.g., the Sons of Liberty and the four Annapolis signers of the Declaration of Independence). In the museum, Braceli, with the help of a team of fabricators, created three enormous murals and two other works. The murals perform an autopsy of the tree. The largest multiplies the tulip poplar's distinctive leaf shape across a 33'-long wall in a wind-swept swirl of energy (the leaves were made from stencils of the Liberty Tree scion's actual leaves). A second mural abstracts the tree's tangled root system into a water-bearing drawing (using PVC tubing) that sprouts purple carnations. The third mural's subject is the tree's massive trunk, which was cut to pieces in 1999, with much of the wood later finding commemorative as Liberty Tree guitars, conference tables, and bible boxes. Onto nine chalkboards, Braceli has mounted nine pieces of raw wood, each supporting live orchids. What can we learn anew from this tree?, it seems to ask. The two other works urge us to turn away from nation-state identities and to look and listen more closely to nature. A sculptural ear is mounted onto the red silhouette of a rose petal, borrowed from the work of Columbia-born, Venezuela-based artist Roberto Obregoń. Nearby, a flag of yellow roses hangs from a flagpole that has been fabricated from a branch. Admission & Hours Free & open to the public Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday, and Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Open Friday, 12 to 7:30 p.m. Parking

events.title: Shifting Boundaries: Perspectives on American Landscapes
events.address: Jefferson Drive at 12th St., SW, Washington, DC
events.description: American painters Willard Metcalf, Dwight Tryon, Winslow Homer, and Abbott Thayer created profoundly beautiful views of the New England landscapes where they lived and worked. These paintings largely depict that environment as timeless and static. Shifting Boundaries looks at these works from a new angle by engaging a multiplicity of voices and viewpoints to explore what these paintings can tell us about changes to this region both past and present. As Shifting Boundaries reveals, the views these artists created of pasturelands in Massachusetts and of seascapes in Maine were transforming even as these artists recorded them. This reshaping of landscapes has only accelerated in the century since Metcalf, Tryon, Homer, and Thayer depicted them. Shifting Boundaries pilots a new mode of collaborative curatorial practice. NMAA Lunder Curator of American Art Diana Greenwold , curatorial assistant Mary Mulcahy , and interpretation specialists Liz Gardner and Amy Freesun partnered with Lauren Brandes (Smithsonian Gardens), Dennis Chestnut (Groundwork Anacostia River DC), Jerome Foster II (Waic Up), Elizabeth James-Perry (Aquinnah Wampanoag artist), Lorette Picciano (Rural Coalition), Stephanie Toothman (National Park Service), and Melinda Whicher (Smithsonian Gardens) to develop the themes for this exhibition, select works of art, and write object labels. The group’s perspectives, drawn from their individual areas of professional expertise and their own personal experiences, allow us to see new details in these stunning works of art. The landscapes become invitations to explore a century of human impact on New England land and water, the erasure of indigenous histories, and the environmental changes that are altering this region today.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away First Responders and Open Captions Show Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life. Content Warning: Some mature content & langage.

events.title: Speaking Truth to Power: The Free Press in a Changing World
events.description: Presented by the MD Two-Fifty Commission. Join us for a special evening of programming and a community conversation about the state of journalism and a free press in the United States. Two hundred fifty years ago, the founders of our country believed that a free press was essential to building and keeping a successful democracy. Freedom of the press, along with freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and the freedom to peacefully assemble and to petition the government, are rights protected by the First Amendment. Yet today, as we celebrate the 250th anniversary of our country’s founding, Americans are watching struggles between the government and the press over exactly what a free press means. Citizens are concerned about court rulings, lawsuits, Justice Department investigations, governmental banning of reporters from news coverage, anti-press statements from government officials, and attacks against journalists. On international surveys, America’s ranking as a country with a free press has dropped significantly. Citizens are left wondering who qualifies as “the press.” Who can citizens trust? What does the future of a free press in America look like in these times? This event brings together an experienced group of journalists to offer insight into these questions. As our keynote speaker, Terry Moran will address these issues head-on. Moran is a veteran American journalist who spent nearly 28 years at ABC News, where he served as Chief White House Correspondent, Chief Foreign Correspondent, co-anchor of Nightline, ABC News Live anchor, and covered the Supreme Court for the network. He is the founder of Real Patriotism, an independent media platform where he currently explores stories about the struggle to find and report truth in the American Democracy. Our panelists for this event include: Ian Cameron – Former Executive Producer for ABC News and the CBC; currently involved as a leader in the free press movement, organizing veteran journalists to take action in s

Attendees can also view the “Revolutionary Maryland: Freedom of the Press Then and Now” exhibition. This community event comes at a crucial point in time, as Americans are watching struggles between the government and the press over exactly what a free press means in 2026. Visitors will get up close to more than 40 original artifacts and documents, including a rare 1823 Stone Engraving of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington's annotated copy of the Constitution, and presidential gifts including horseshoes to President Bush from Queen Elizabeth II. The American Story will be the first and only museum in Washington, DC to use artificial intelligence (AI) to bring each visitor a special, individualized opportunity to explore the records of the American people and engage with American history. This exhibit brings more than two million historic records to life, offering a personalized journey through our nation's past. This new museum experience provides all Americans with a special opportunity to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.

events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: We Make History
events.description: As the nation commemorates 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence, "We Make History" explores how history happens, is preserved and shared. In Washington, D.C. and places around the country, many people were quietly keeping the records, building the collections, and developing the skills that would create America’s historical narrative. These community-based stories serve as the building blocks for 250 years of American history. Using the country’s anniversary as a milestone, the museum uses its community driven practice to celebrate local civic engagement and encourage local history keeping. This exhibition is a tribute to celebrating our communities and making possible a better understanding of our shared past. These stories are important to marking the Semiquincentennial because they help show the legacy of how people make history one act, one document, one story at a time. By bringing these stories to the forefront in 2026, the exhibit inspires the next generation to keep and share their own stories and records to add to America’s historical narrative. We Make History has an anticipated opening date of May 30, 2026.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Blitzkid
events.description: Horror punk legends BLITZKID return to the road this fall in support of their long-awaited new studio album, MODERN HEL, their first full length release in sixteen years. Formed in 1997, Blitzkid quickly became one of the most influential bands in modern horror punk and has remained one of the genre’s leading exponents. Known for their driving punk energy, dark atmosphere, and unforgettable melodic hooks, the band has built an international following through decades of touring across the globe. From Wave Gotik Treffen to Wacken Open Air, Blitzkid’s versatility has allowed them to perform at some of the world’s most notable genre festivals, demonstrating the band’s unique ability to connect with audiences across multiple underground scenes. With MODERN HEL, Blitzkid enters a powerful new chapter. While the band’s signature haunting melodies and anthemic choruses remain firmly intact, the new material pushes their sound into more aggressive territory, incorporating a blistering fusion of thrash and hardcore to a degree the band has never explored before. The result is a blistering blend of driving riffs and haunting hooks that have defined Blitzkid for nearly three decades. MODERN HE

events.title: Camp One Heartland
events.description: Camp One Heartland is a solo exhibition by Tye DuSold-O’Connor archiving documentation of one of the world’s first nonprofit summer camps designated to supporting and empowering youth affected by HIV and AIDS, eventually transforming into a vital beacon of safety, liberation and eutopia for LGBTQ+ youth across the country. After its inaugural session in the summer of 1993 and many more held at different campsites across the country, Camp One Heartland found its permanent residence in Willow River, Minnesota. Over the next three decades it broadened its reach to provide summer camp sessions for youth experiencing housing instability, LGBTQ+ youth, and specifically trans youth. Tye attended Camp One Heartland as both a camper in 2022 and a counselor in 2024, and found these experiences indescribably transformative to them and their queer identity. Quite suddenly, Camp One Heartland shut down permanently in the fall of 2024 due to financial issues. Former campers, counselors and staff have been unable to return to the site since. While camp counseling in the summer of 2024, Tye took hundreds of photos of the camp, its people, and its experiences. These serve as some of the last images taken during the lifetime of Camp One Heartland. Artist Bio: Tye DuSold-O’Connor is a multimedia artist studying Fine Art and Psychology whose work revolves around trans experience, identity and culture. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: CENTENNIAL FILM Series: Cabin in the Sky (1943)
events.description: A Musical Battle Between Good & Evil Cabin in the Sky follows Little Joe, a man who, after being killed over gambling debts, awakens in purgatory and is granted six months back on Earth to redeem himself and prove he deserves entry into Heaven. His journey through faith, love, and moral conflict unfolds through a series of musical performances that reflect both earthly temptation and heavenly intervention. Featuring music by Duke Ellington and his Orchestra , Cabin in the Sky blends gospel, jazz, and theatrical storytelling into a rich stylized musical fantasy. The film is notable for its all-Black cast, making it an important early example of mainstream Hollywood representation during the Golden Age of cinema. Combining vivid fantasy sequences, moral allegory, and elaborate musical staging, Cabin in the Sky remains a visually striking and culturally significant work celebrated for its artistry, performances, and lasting historical importance. STARS: Lena Horne, Ethel Waters, Eddie Anderson, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong RUNTIME: 97 minutes GENRE: Musical, Comedy This show is part of the Weinberg Center’s Centennial Film Event, celebrating 100 years of screenings in our historic building. The Weinberg Center , located in the heart of Downtown Frederick, MD, offers a historic backdrop and timeless atmosphere for a unique film experience.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Forest Germans between Geography, History and Memory: Mapping a Forgotten Settlement Region in Southern Poland
events.description: One of the most intriguing paradoxes in Central European history is that a Polish cultural and territorial community is known as the Forest Germans, a name reflecting the complexity of its identity and history. The Forest Germans emerged through centuries of cultural and biological synthesis, combining German influences with West Slavic and, above all, Polish elements. Their history dates back to the 14th century, when medieval German newcomers and West Slavic settlers from Germania Slavica, through intermingling with the Polish population, gradually underwent complete Polonization between the 16th and 18th centuries. Through assimilation, acculturation, adaptation, and cultural exchange, the Forest Germans emerged as a distinct cultural group in Poland not later than in the 17th century. Today, their descendants live in the northern Carpathians in south-eastern Poland, where Polish and German surnames, place names, and family histories intertwine. Marcin Wojciech Solarz, PhD, the IR researcher at the Faculty of Geography and Regional Studies of the University of Warsaw, Poland will give a lecture examining the history, ethnonym, and settlement boundaries of Forest Germany. He distinguishes the broader region, known as Great Forest Germany, from the narrower settlement area, Small Forest Germany, divided into at least three settlement enclaves: Biecz, Krosno, and Łańcut. events.title: Indecent: The True Story of a Little Jewish Play
events.description: ASL Sign Interpreted Performance and Afterword discussion on Friday, November 20 . Written by Paula Vogel, Score and Original Music by Lisa Gutkin and Aaron Halva Directed by Sasha Olinick Performances will be held in the Theatre Arts Arena on the Montgomery College Rockville campus. In 1906 a young, up and coming Jewish/Polish writer, Sholem Asch, penned “God of Vengeance”, a play attacking religious hypocrisy and lovingly depicting a romantic relationship between two women. The play quickly became a hit as it toured throughout Europe and was translated from its original Yiddish into several different languages. But in America, when an English translation opened on Broadway in 1923, the play was quickly shut down and the cast, director and producer were jailed and prosecuted for violating obscenity laws. Indecent, by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Paula Vogel, charts the history of this incendiary drama and the path of the artists who risked their careers and lives to perform it. INDECENT is presented by arrangement with Concord Theatricals on behalf of Dramatists Play Service. Indecent is recommended for mature audiences and teenagers aged 13 and older due to adult themes and historical prejudice.

events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: One Moses, Two Scriptures: The Torah and the Qur'an in Conversation
events.description: The Torah and the Qur'an tell stories about many of the same figures — above all, Moses, the prophet the Qur'an names more often than any other. For fourteen centuries, Jews and Muslims have interpreted these stories through traditions in each other's shadow, amid rivalry, exchange and mutual influence. What happens when they are read side by side? Join GW's Ambassador John L. Loeb, Jr. Institute for Religious Freedom and Democracy for a discussion about what the two scriptures share, where they diverge and what reading them together can — and cannot — do for Jews and Muslims today. Speakers: Rick Sopher (Woolf Institute) is co-author (with Abdulla Galadari) of the recently published Illuminating Scriptural Connections: A Qur'anic Commentary on the Torah (Jewish Publication Society, 2026), which reads every weekly Torah portion alongside the Qur'an.Mustafa Akyol (Cato Institute), author of The Islamic Moses: How the Prophet Inspired Jews and Muslims to Flourish Together and Change the World (St. Martin's, 2024), has explored the common religious grammar of law, prophecy and scholarship that has connected Judaism and Islam across the centuries.Historian of Islam Joel Blecher, associate professor of history at George Washington University, is a scholar of Islamic intellectual history and traditions of textual interpretation.RSVP >>

events.description: Python Camp is a non-credit, hands-on, intensive mini-course offered by GW Libraries and Academic Innovation (LAI) for the GW community. Python Camp introduces foundational programming practice using the Python language, with a focus on building skill through both team-based activities and self-guided exercises. The aim is to expose participants to the core concepts of programming, while providing a sufficient foundation in Python syntax and programming patterns to allow participants to build upon their learning in other contexts. Participation is free for members of the GW community, though application is required. Applications are due by September 21, 2026, and applicants will be notified approximately two weeks after the deadline. While we are not able to offer academic credit, participants who successfully complete Python Camp will receive a certificate of completion from LAI. Participants should expect to spend at 4 hours a day learning together, and at least 1-2 hours per day doing self-guided homework. Additional assistance with homework is available throughout the Camp. All sessions are free to GW students, faculty, and staff. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life.

Read more about the exhibitions below: Unfossilizing African Art: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: The Great War and Great Flu Come to the Mother Continent
events.address: 400 Ferndale Ave., Hodson Auditorium, Rosenstock Hall, Frederick, MD 21701
events.description: The First World War began in Africa on Aug 3, 1914, six days after hostilities began in Europe. Across the continent, the miserable yoke of European imperialism was felt by local people forced into a conflict they did not ask for. Join us for an immersive historical evening exploring one of World War I’s most grueling theaters. We will screen “Chasing the Phantom”, a 2007 Lucasfilm documentary that follows the legendary campaign of German General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, the "Lion of Africa", who led a guerrilla campaign with African askaris through German East Africa. His forces evaded capture throughout the war, surrendering only two weeks after the 1918 Armistice. Scott Hileman Ph.D. will begin the evening with an overview of the African theater. After the film, we will discuss WWI’s devastating impact on the continent, including the 1918 influenza pandemic, with historians Anne Samson Ph.D. and Peter Doyle, Ph.D. The Great Flu would inflict a terrible toll on both the Lion’s malnourished troops and on the African peoples, one often overlooked in tales of WWI. Hosted by Department of Biology as part of International Education Week 2026. Co-sponsored by Center for Global Studies & the Graduate School. Refreshments will be provided. Admission is free and open to all. Please RSVP to Mark Chee Ph.D., chee@hood.edu Can't join us in person? Please register for a Zoom invitation at https://tinyurl.com/mph-film-fest

events.title: The Importance of Climate Leadership and the Power of Public Action
events.description: Al Gore and Rep. Maxwell Frost discuss climate, democracy, affordability and their hopes for the future. Twenty years ago, former Vice President Al Gore and The Climate Reality Project set out to turn everyday citizens into leaders. Today, we find ourselves posing the question: with a new Congress, will there be fresh opportunities for progress? This is an in-person event. No livestream will be available. Vice President Gore, who has spent decades pushing the climate crisis to the center of public debate, is joined by Congressman Maxwell Frost, a longtime organizer who brings the urgency of a new generation to Capitol Hill. Together, they’ll hold a cross-generational conversation on the road ahead: the policy priorities facing lawmakers, the payoffs clean energy is already delivering, and the ways an engaged citizenry and organizations like Climate Reality are standing up to the fossil fuel industry and turning ambition into change.

events.description: Join Free Minds Book Club & Writing Workshop for a special advance screening of “Verses from the Inside,” an episode from The Poet Speaks Season 2: We Speak What Was , ahead of its broadcast premiere on PBS and Heritage Broadcasting. A conversation follows the screening with Free Minds poets and host Amanda Eke. About the Episode Episode 2, “Verses from the Inside,” follows host Amanda Eke inside a Washington, D.C. correctional facility, where poetry becomes a lifeline, a way to process, reflect, and reclaim a voice in a place designed to take so much of that voice away. The episode then follows Free Minds poets who have carried that practice beyond incarceration and into their lives as artists and advocates. From inside the walls to life beyond them, Verses from the Inside asks what poetry can make possible when words become a means of survival, connection, and transformation. About the Series The Poet Speaks is a documentary-style series hosted by Amanda Eke that explores the power of poetry as a cultural and historical force. Season 2, We Speak What Was , is a six-episode journey through Washington, D.C., where poetry, music, memory, history, and community collide. Support Free Minds This event is free and open to all. A donation alone does not reserve a seat. To attend and support Free Minds Book Club & Writing Workshop, select both a free admission ticket and an optional donation.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Camelot
events.description: Welcome to CAMELOT! Borrowing from the Arthurian legends, CAMELOT is Lerner and Loewe's fantastical masterpiece. An idealistic King Arthur hopes to create a kingdom built on honor and dignity, embodied by his Knights of The Round Table. He establishes an order built on using “might for right.” His ideals, however, are tested when his lovely queen, Guenevere, falls in love with his most loyal knight, Lancelot. Add in the dastardly Mordred and his wicked schemes and it soon appears this dream of a kingdom may only exist for one brief, shining moment. ​ This stirring Golden Age musical has enchanted generations of theatregoers with its sweeping score and iconic characters. It is a romance, a tragedy, a comedy, an adventure, a fantasy, and a stirring exploration of power and leadership all at once. And above all, it is a piece about the stories and ideals we pass along to future generations.​

events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Cult of Love-Round House Theatre
events.description: Celebrate the holidays with the Broadway sensation Cult of Love ! In this gripping, music-filled play, four adult siblings (and their partners) return home for Christmas Eve, carrying secrets, resentments, and competing ideas of what family demands. As the singing and celebration give way to confrontation, old wounds reopen and new revelations emerge. Leslye Headland’s “stormy, compassionate, [and] cuttingly observant” ( TimeOut NY ) play interrogates the complexity of family loyalty, the power of religion, and what it truly means to love one another.

events.title: Disney Frozen the Broadway Musical
events.description: Disney’s Frozen the Broadway Musical brings the beloved animated film to the stage in a breathtaking theatrical event filled with heart, humor, and unforgettable music. When the newly crowned Queen Elsa accidentally unleashes a winter that threatens to trap her kingdom in eternal ice, her fearless sister Anna sets off on a daring journey to find her and save Arendelle. Along the way, Anna teams up with rugged ice harvester Kristoff, his loyal reindeer Sven, and the ever-optimistic snowman Olaf in an adventure that tests the meaning of love, loyalty, and sacrifice. Featuring dazzling costumes, spectacular scenic effects, and expanded storytelling created especially for the stage, Frozen goes beyond the film to deepen the bond between the sisters at its core. The musical includes beloved songs such as “Let It Go,” “Do You Want to Build a Snowman?” and “For the First Time in Forever,” alongside thrilling new numbers written exclusively for Broadway. A powerful tale of self-acceptance and the unbreakable strength of family, Frozen the Broadway Musical is a magical, uplifting experience for audiences of all ages. Disney’s Frozen is presented through special arrangement with Music Theatre International (MTI). All authorized performance materials are also supplied by MTI. mtishows.com

events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Fort DeRussy Civil War Hike: Defending the Capital
events.description: Join a ranger for a guided hike to Fort DeRussy, a Civil War site in Washington, DC. As you walk through the wooded landscape of Rock Creek Park, you’ll uncover how this fort helped protect the nation’s capital during a time of conflict. Along the way, learn about the soldiers who lived and worked here and the challenges they faced while stationed in the field. At the fort, explore the earthworks that still stand today and imagine what life was like inside this military post. Rangers will share stories of daily routines, military strategy, and the experiences of those who served here. This hike offers a chance to experience history where it happened while connecting with the natural landscape that surrounds it. This program begins at the Rock Creek Park Nature Center.

events.title: Gallery B Presents “Intersections | Realism & Abstraction”
events.description: “ INTERSECTIONS ⎸ Realism & Abstraction” is a group exhibition featuring four artists – Lawrence Chandler, Angela Iovino, Ariana Progri, and Ravi Raman – with distinct art styles in conversation with each other, showing that even the most realistic art is a form of abstraction (a reduction of reality) and that abstract art can hold elements of structural, grounded reality. Instead of treating realism and abstraction as binary opposites, works in the exhibition also intersect both worlds, showcasing how different artists navigate the spectrum between the two styles. Viewers not only will see realistic figures and recognizable subjects dissolving into, or emerging from abstract backgrounds, but also the use of bold brushstrokes, form, color, and textures to convey emotion rather than literal details.

events.title: Indecent: The True Story of a Little Jewish Play
events.description: ASL Sign Interpreted Performance and Afterword discussion on Friday, November 20 . Written by Paula Vogel, Score and Original Music by Lisa Gutkin and Aaron Halva Directed by Sasha Olinick Performances will be held in the Theatre Arts Arena on the Montgomery College Rockville campus. In 1906 a young, up and coming Jewish/Polish writer, Sholem Asch, penned “God of Vengeance”, a play attacking religious hypocrisy and lovingly depicting a romantic relationship between two women. The play quickly became a hit as it toured throughout Europe and was translated from its original Yiddish into several different languages. But in America, when an English translation opened on Broadway in 1923, the play was quickly shut down and the cast, director and producer were jailed and prosecuted for violating obscenity laws. Indecent, by Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Paula Vogel, charts the history of this incendiary drama and the path of the artists who risked their careers and lives to perform it. INDECENT is presented by arrangement with Concord Theatricals on behalf of Dramatists Play Service. Indecent is recommended for mature audiences and teenagers aged 13 and older due to adult themes and historical prejudice.

events.description: Modern classics don’t come any bigger than Les Misérables, and Olney Theatre celebrates it for the first time in honor of the show’s 40th anniversary. Follow Jean-Valjean from his beginnings as convict #24601 to life in hiding, to protector of Cosette, pursued all the while by the relentless Javert, culminating in the revolutionary passions of the 1832 Paris uprising. events.title: Lonesome River Band
events.description: It’s hard to think of a genre more committed to sustained creative careers than bluegrass. Case in point: the 41-years-and-counting path of Mountain Home Music Company stalwarts, Lonesome River Band. Though the last remaining original member departed before the turn of the century, the group — a quintet for more than 20 years now — hasn’t so much reinvented itself as refined a profoundly influential signature sound that has a seemingly endless appeal to successive generations of fans and musicians alike. Led by 30-plus year veteran and award-winning banjo man Sammy Shelor, who has presided over one stellar lineup after another, LRB remains among the genre’s most widely admired and powerful draws, both in person and on streaming platforms.

events.title: Michael McDermott
events.description: Jammin' Java welcomes singer-songwriter Michael McDermott on Thursday, November 20th, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. at 227 Maple Avenue in Vienna, Fairfax County, Virginia. Chicago native McDermott has occupied a peculiar and essential place in American music for thirty-plus years: extravagantly praised by Stephen King, The Washington Post, and The Hollywood Reporter, yet perpetually on the verge of the recognition his artistry demands. Raised on the dual gospel of early Dylan and the Stones, Tom Waits and the Who, Woody Guthrie and Van Morrison, McDermott has never made a record that fits neatly into a marketing category—a restless refusal to be contained that makes him essential. His forthcoming album Flowers From The Graveyard (arriving August 21, 2027) collects 11 self-penned songs moving fluidly between anthemic rock and bruised introspection, between political fury and hard-won philosophical calm. The Hollywood Reporter notes "Despair never sounded so good," while Stephen King calls him "one of the best songwriters in the world." The Washington Post suggests "McDermott may prove to be one of his generation's greatest talents." This intimate performance delivers the uncompromising songwriting, raw emotional depth, and masterful artistry that define one of America's most important voices. Admission is $34.00 plus fees. Michael McDermott combines lyrical excellence, unflinching humanity, and timeless rock 'n' roll soul in Fairfax County, Virginia. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: New Players, Old Plays? Continuity and Change in Development Diplomacy
events.venue: School of Media and Public Affairs
events.description: Overview Are emerging powers reshaping international development cooperation or playing by the existing rules? Abstract The growing participation of emerging powers in international development cooperation raises questions about the changing nature of development diplomacy. As these actors expand their roles as donors, are they challenging established practices and structures, or reproducing them? More broadly, does the arrival of new actors necessarily change how development diplomacy is practiced and understood? This talk explores these questions through two ongoing research projects that examine the structural and communicative dimensions of development diplomacy. The first study, Claiming a Seat at the Table: Legitimacy Narratives of Emerging Donors in Development Diplomacy, examines how China, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey communicate their roles as development actors to general public. Through a quantitative content analysis of 832 social media posts from their respective development agencies, the study explores whether emerging donors advance alternative narratives of development cooperation or seek legitimacy through established frameworks and expectations. The second project, The Changing Architecture of Green Energy Assistance: A Network Analysis of Emerging Powers 2 , uses social network analysis of international green-technology assistance between 2012 and 2023 to examine whether emerging powers are reshaping established patterns of cooperation. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: South Lakes Theatre Arts Presents Come From Away
events.description: Come From Away, written by Irene Sankoff and David Hein, is a critically acclaimed musical featuring a poignantly relevant script and a deeply moving score. The show’s global presence resonates across all audiences as an uplifting reminder of humanity’s ability to come together, no matter what the circumstances. Based on real events of September 11th, 2001, Come From Away tells the story in which 38 planes, carrying thousands of passengers from across the globe, were diverted to the isolated community of Gander, Newfoundland. The locals of the small town played host to the world as they fed, housed, and comforted the stranded passengers for over four days. Inundated by culture clashes and language barriers, the people of Gander persevered, demonstrating the power of kindness. On the 10 th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011, Sankoff and Hein traveled to Gander to interview residents and returning passengers. They turned hundreds of distinct accounts into a celebrated musical. For this 25 th anniversary year of September 11th, South Lakes Theatre Arts is honored to bring these accounts to life. Content Warning: Some mature content & langage. Disclaimer: There will be NO intermission for this production.

events.title: Transgender Day of Remembrance and Resilience (TDORR)
events.description: Friday, November 20th—Join us for Trans Day of Remembrance and Resilience (TDORR), a day of COMMUNITY POWER when we honor the memories of transgender people whose lives were lost in acts of violence this year. What is TDOR? From GLAAD : the first Transgender Day of Remembrance (TDOR) was started in 1999 by transgender advocate Gwendolyn Ann Smith as a vigil to honor the memory of Rita Hester, a transgender woman killed in 1998. The vigil commemorated all the transgender people lost to violence since Rita Hester’s death, and began an important tradition that has become the annual Transgender Day of Remembrance. In a 2012 article with Huffpost , Smith is quoted as saying, “the right to simply exist is first and foremost. With so many seeking to erase transgender people — sometimes in the most brutal ways possible — it is vitally important that those we lose are remembered, and that we continue to fight for justice.” Why the 2nd “R”? While not entirely widespread (yet), the MoCo Pride Family uses the moniker “TDORR” to underscore gratitude as essential to our celebration of transgender lives. On the Transgender Day of Remembrance, we honor those we have lost and those that continue to live in the face of violence, oppression, and all other forces turned against our community. Transgender people are brave — we will survive, and we will do so with our ancestors and martyrs in our hearts. events.title: Triangle Art Studios Presents “Luminance: Contained” by Susan Darrow
events.description: “Luminance Contained ” will feature black & white works by Rockville-based fine art photographer Susan Darrow. Darrow first picked up a camera in high school, learning old-school techniques of darkroom developing and printing. She uses a full-format digital camera with a large sensor to capture maximum sharp detail, and carefully composes the best possible photograph in-camera, minimizing post-production editing. Darrow is drawn to Black & White Photography because of the stability and order it brings to what was once a chaotic scene. “The tones are all connected to each other, and what was once a jostling combustion of color at once becomes peaceful.” The exhibition runs November 20 through December 27. Gallery hours are Fridays & Saturdays, 10am – 5pm; Sundays, 11am – 2pm. There will be an opening reception Saturday, November 21, 5 – 8pm. The exhibit will also be open for the Bethesda Art Walk on Friday, December 11, 6 – 8pm.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.description: Virginia helped shape the beginnings of our nation, and local audiences can experience the drama, humor and music behind America’s founding in 1776 , the Tony Award-winning musical presented by The Pickwick Players. Just in time for America’s 250th anniversary, 1776 takes audiences inside the Continental Congress, where John Adams pushes for independence, Benjamin Franklin brings his wit and wisdom, and Virginia’s own Thomas Jefferson is called upon to put the revolutionary cause into words. The story also features Richard Henry Lee of Virginia, whose resolution calling for independence helped move the colonies toward a historic decision. What happens when a room full of passionate, stubborn and politically divided men try to agree on the future of a nation? There’s plenty of debate, a little scheming, larger-than-life personalities and some unforgettable music. With music and lyrics by Sherman Edwards and a book by Peter Stone, 1776 combines clever dialogue, colorful characters, political maneuvering and a memorable score. From the spirited opening number, “Sit Down, John,” to the lively “The Lees of Old Virginia” and the stirring “Is Anybody There?,” the music captures the humor, frustrations and high stakes behind the birth of a nation. Forget the dusty history books. 1776 presents the founding fathers as real people, with big egos, strong opinions, competing interests and a monumental decision to make. events.title: A Raisin in the Sun
events.description: The Younger family on Chicago’s South Side is holding tight to visions of a brighter future, but when a life insurance check arrives, suddenly possibility comes with a price. Sat Nov 21 2:00pm To – 4:30pm The Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center Buy Tickets Clarice website Add to Calendar “What happens to a dream deferred? / Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?” - Langston Hughes The Younger family on Chicago’s South Side is holding tight to visions of a brighter future. When a life insurance check arrives, suddenly possibility comes with a price. As each family member reaches for a different dream, they must confront what a better life really means – and what America is willing to share. Both tender and electrifying, A Raisin in the Sun celebrates Black joy, resilience and family while facing the brutal realities of segregation and discrimination. A landmark of American theater, it made history as the first Broadway play written by an African American woman (Lorraine Hansberry), the first Broadway play directed by an African American man (Lloyd Richards), and the first commercially produced Broadway drama to center Black life. TDPS Assistant Professor KenYatta Rogers (director of Stick Fly, Men on Boats , Metamorphoses and Home ) directs this enduring American classic. Location The Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center 8270 Alumni Drive College Pa

events.title: Autumn in Watercolor: A Fall Painting Workshop @ Lost Rhino Brewery
events.description: Spend a cozy fall evening slowing down, sipping, and exploring watercolor at Lost Rhino Brewery! This three-hour beginner-friendly workshop is designed to be a full creative experience, giving you the time to learn, experiment, and complete two fall-inspired paintings: a colorful birch tree landscape and a sweet pumpkin/ gourd “Thankful” card to take home. Led by a professional practicing artist and painter, you’ll be guided step-by-step while learning approachable watercolor techniques along the way. We’ll explore how to work with water and pigment, build layers, create texture, and embrace the beautiful, fluid nature of watercolor. No painting experience is needed, and there will be plenty of room to make each piece feel like your own. More than just leaving with two finished paintings, the goal of this workshop is to give you a foundation you can take with you. You’ll leave with new skills, a better understanding of watercolor, and hopefully a new creative outlet you can continue enjoying long after the class is over. All painting materials are included, plus each ticket includes a beverage from the bar to sip while you paint. Come settle in for three cozy hours of painting, learning, and creating something inspired by the season.

events.description: NOTE: This is a parent and child workshop, cost of a seat get you and one child into the workshop to make 2 ornaments together. In this festive hands-on workshop, Maria of Beaver Creek Cottage Garden will guide you through crafting a charming collection of handmade ornaments using materials straight from nature. All materials provided. Space is limited — register early to secure your spot! MEET MARIA Maria has a BS degree in Biology from the University of Maryland plus an MS degree in Pharmacognosy from the University of Rhode Island. She founded Willow Oak Flower + Herb Farm over 40 years ago, which has been featured in Baltimore Bride, Washingtonian Weddings, Capitol Romance and Maryland Farm & Harvest. She taught at Tai Sophia (now known as Maryland University of Integrative Health) and Continuing Education at Anne Arundel Community College for over 30 years. events.title: Cocoa, Cookies & Cows | A Highland Cow + Valais Sheep  Holiday Experience
events.description: Cocoa, Cookies & Cows | A Highland Cow + Valais Sheep Holiday Experience One of Scarlet Springs Farm’s most beloved holiday traditions is back! Cocoa, Cookies & Cows invites you to spend a festive afternoon with our adorable Highland cows, calves, Valais sheep, and lambs before warming up with homemade hot cocoa and cookies in our beautifully decorated Ridgetop Stable. Your experience begins with a 30-minute group animal immersion, where you’ll have the chance to pet, brush, feed, and love on our friendly Highland cows and calves, along with our famously puppy-dog-friendly Valais sheep and lambs. While the animals don’t mind sharing their barn, this portion of the experience will be largely outdoors, so please dress accordingly. After enjoying the highlands & lambs, we’ll clean up and then head down to the Ridgetop Stable, where you can warm up in our heated, enclosed space for the remaining hour while taking in the sweeping views of the farm. For the holidays, the stable will be transformed with festive décor and music to create the perfect cozy holiday setting. Settle in with your family, sip on homemade hot cocoa, enjoy a tower of delicious cookies, and soak up what makes Scarlet Springs so special. Before you head home, be sure to stop by The Scarlet Shop for Highland-inspired Christmas gifts and keepsakes. Whether this is your first visit or an annual family tradition, Cocoa, Cookies & Cows is the perfect way to slow down, get cozy, and make holiday memories together.​ ​What’s Included with Your Ticket: 1.5 hour experience on the beautiful 74-acre Scarlet Springs Far 30 minutes with the Highlands — pet, brush, feed, and meet our fluffy, friendly Highland cows and calves Time with our Valais sheep and lambs Seat with your party in our festive, beautifully decorated and heated Ridgetop Stable Homemade hot cocoa and cookies Sweeping views of the farm and a festive holiday atmosphere
